transcript:
**Ser Kael** (turn 0):
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

**Squire** (turn 1):
"Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

**Ser Kael** (turn 2):
Ser Kael finished the sequence. He held the final thrust for three slow heartbeats, his muscles steady despite the biting cold, before lowering the practice blade. Only then did he turn his head to look at the squire. His face was set like the gray stone of the keep, showing neither approval for the early work nor irritation at the interruption.

"A knight does not 'think' he got a guard wrong. He knows it," Kael said, his voice flat and raspy from the morning chill. He did not offer a word of praise for the completed stable chores; duty required no reward. 

He stepped back, planting his boots firmly on the frosted cobbles, and held the wooden sword at his side.

"Take your weapon. Assume the stance. Let me see where your discipline failed you."

**Squire** (turn 3):
*I gulp, my breath pluming in the cold air.* "Yes, Ser." I hurry to grab my own practice sword, the wood cold against my fingers. *I try to remember the footwork, the exact angle of the blade.* "Like this?" I ask, my voice a bit shaky, holding the sword up.

**Ser Kael** (turn 4):
Ser Kael did not answer immediately. He walked a slow circle around the squire, his boots crunching on the thin frost. His eyes, sharp and unforgiving, dissected the boy's posture from the heel to the tip of the wooden blade. 

He stopped in front of the squire. Without warning, Kael tapped the flat of his own practice sword sharply against the squire's elbow, forcing it upward.

"Your elbow is sagging. A real blade would have sheared it off by now," Kael said, his voice as biting as the wind. He nudged the heel of the squire's back boot with his own toe, widening the stance. "Your weight is too far forward. If I pushed you now, you would fall like a sack of barley. Lower your center."

He stepped back, his hands resting on the pommel of his sheathed broadsword, his gaze steady and demanding.

"And stop your shaking. A knight who fears the cold will surely freeze in the face of steel. Hold the position. Do not move until I tell you."

**Squire** (turn 5):
I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

**Ser Kael** (turn 6):
Ser Kael did not move to assist the boy. He stood over his squire, a tall, unyielding silhouette against the pale morning light, his arms crossed over his chest. His face remained as hard and emotionless as the stone walls of the keep.

"Get up," Kael said, his voice flat and commanding. "A knight kneels before his liege, and he kneels before his God. He does not kneel before his own fatigue."

He looked down at the squire, his gaze cold and dissecting. 

"I do not 'need' you to be anything," Kael continued, refusing to offer even a shred of comfort. "Your strength is not for my benefit. It is for your own survival. The enemy will not pause to let you catch your breath, nor will they show mercy because you apologized."

He tapped the toe of his boot against the flat of the squire's discarded wooden sword.

"Pick up the blade. Stand. We have half an hour before the morning chapel. Use it."

**Squire** (turn 7):
*I wince, but scramble to my feet, grabbing the practice sword.* My muscles ache already. "Yes, Ser." *I try to remember the stance again, forcing my body into position even though I want to collapse.* "What... what should we work on now?"

**Ser Kael** (turn 8):
Ser Kael watched the squire struggle back to his feet. He did not offer a hand, nor did his expression soften at the boy's obvious physical exhaustion. To Kael, pain was merely information—a sign that the body was weak and required further tempering. 

He walked a slow, deliberate half-circle around the boy, inspecting the re-established stance. It was sloppy, born of tired muscles, but the boy was standing. That was the bare minimum expected of him.

"You ask what we should work on, as if you have mastered the first lesson," Kael said, his voice level and dry. "We work on the high guard. Again."

He raised his own wooden practice blade, holding it loosely in one hand. 

"A man does not build a castle by laying the roof before the foundation is set. Your foundation is shaking," Kael continued, his gaze locking onto the squire's eyes. "Hold the guard. I will strike your blade three times. If your grip falters, or if you yield a single step backward, you will spend your evening scrubbing the armory floor after vespers. Raise the weapon."

**Squire** (turn 9):
*My jaw tightens.* "Yes, Ser." *I lift my sword, trying to keep my arms steady despite the tremble in my legs.* Scrubbing the armory floor sounds awful. I focus on his eyes, trying to anticipate his first strike.

**Ser Kael** (turn 10):
Ser Kael did not shift his stance, nor did he allow any tell to show in his posture before he moved. He noted the squire's intense focus on his face.

"You look at my eyes," Kael said, his voice flat. "A common error. A man can lie with his eyes. He can feint with his gaze. Watch the center of my chest. The shoulders do not lie."

Without further warning, Kael stepped forward. He did not swing with his full strength—that would be senseless—but he struck with the heavy, unyielding force of a seasoned soldier. The wooden practice sword came down in a sharp, diagonal slice aimed directly at the squire's high guard. 

The crack of wood meeting wood echoed sharply in the quiet, frosty yard. Kael did not immediately disengage; he kept his blade pressed against the squire's for a fraction of a second, testing the resistance, checking if the boy's wrists would buckle under the sudden weight.

"That is one," Kael murmured, his face inches from the squire's, his breath cold. "Brace your core. The second will be heavier."

**Squire** (turn 11):
"Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

**Ser Kael** (turn 12):
Ser Kael did not answer. Instead, his eyes narrowed slightly at the lapse in focus. 

Before the squire could even finish the sentence, Kael disengaged his blade, stepped back half a pace, and delivered the second strike. It was faster and heavier than the first, a sharp, downward blow meant to punish the boy's split-second distraction. 

The crack of wood on wood was louder this time, sending a jarring vibration down the squire's arms.

"You ask questions because your lungs burn and you seek a reprieve," Kael said, his voice flat and entirely unaffected by the boy's attempt at conversation. "And you ask 'why' as if a man has a choice in his duty."

He did not lower his weapon. He stood in his guard, his face a mask of cold indifference. 

"My father sent me to page at eight years of age. I was knighted at twenty because my lord required swords and my faith demanded service. There is no grander tale, squire. There is only the vow, the shield, and the dirt."

He adjusted his grip on the hilt of his practice sword, his knuckles white in the morning frost. 

"Your mind is wandering to fairy tales while my blade is at your throat. That is two. Prepare for the third."

**Squire** (turn 13):
*I bite my lip, trying to steady my shaking arms.* My wrists sting from the impact. "Yes, Ser." *I try to focus, to push the ache from my mind.* Fairy tales... I just wanted to know.

**Ser Kael** (turn 14):
Ser Kael heard the quiet murmur, but his face did not soften. A squire's curiosity was a useless thing on a battlefield; it did not stop arrows, nor did it blunt steel. 

"Wanting to know is a luxury of those who have already survived the day," Kael said, his voice dropping an octave, cold and final. "You have not survived it yet."

Without another word, he delivered the third strike. It was a heavy, sweeping blow from the left, designed to test the lateral strength of the squire's guard and the stability of his tired legs. Kael put his weight into the swing—not enough to break bone, but more than enough to shatter a weak grip. 

The heavy crack of the wooden training swords rang out through the empty yard. Kael held his follow-through, his blade pressed firmly against the squire's, waiting to see if the boy's wrists would give way or if his boots would slip on the frost.

"Hold," Kael commanded, his eyes locked on the boy's straining posture. "Do not yield an inch."

**Squire** (turn 15):
*My arms burn, my teeth clenched against the pain as I struggle to hold the blade.* My feet slide a little on the frost, but I manage to stay upright. "I won't, Ser," I grunt, my voice strained.

**Ser Kael** (turn 16):
Ser Kael maintained the heavy pressure of his blade for one final, grueling heartbeat, forcing the squire to bear the entirety of his weight. Then, with a sudden, fluid motion, he disengaged, drawing his practice sword back and returning to a relaxed but perfectly poised stance. 

He did not offer a hand. He did not smile. 

His eyes drifted down to the scuff marks in the frost where the squire's boots had slid. 

"Your feet slipped," Kael observed, his voice flat and devoid of pity. "On a muddy field, that slip would have put you on your back with a dagger in your visor. Remember that the earth beneath you is as much your enemy as the man in front of you."

He sheathed his wooden practice sword in the leather loop at his belt. He took a slow breath, his chest rising and falling evenly, showing none of the exhaustion that plagued the boy.

"However, you did not drop the weapon, and you did not retreat," Kael said. It was not a compliment; it was merely a statement of fact. "You did adequate work holding the line. No more."

The distant, heavy tolling of the chapel bell began to ring through the crisp morning air, signaling the start of the morning service. 

Kael turned his back on the squire, walking toward the rack to retrieve his cloak. He slung the heavy, dark wool over his shoulders and fastened it with a simple iron clasp.

"Go to the well," Kael commanded, not looking back. "Wash the sweat and dirt from your face. We do not enter the house of the Father looking like beaten dogs. You have ten minutes to present yourself at the chapel doors, clean and silent. Do not be late."

**Squire** (turn 17):
It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

**Ser Kael** (turn 18):
Ser Kael paused. He had already turned toward the weapon rack, but the lack of immediate movement behind him made him stop. He looked back over his shoulder, his sharp eyes instantly locking onto the boy’s hands, which were trembling against the hilt of the wooden training blade. 

To Kael, a shaking hand was a broken tool. It was a liability on the field and a sign of a mind divided. He did not know of the squire's silent grief, nor would he have altered his conduct if he did; death was a constant companion to their station, and duty did not halt for the dead.

He turned his body fully, his heavy wool cloak settling around his armor. He walked back toward the boy, his boots crunching deliberately on the thin ice. 

"The weapon is sheathed when the drill is done," Kael said, his voice low, flat, and entirely devoid of warmth. "And yet you cling to it as if it were a crutch. If your hands shake from the exertion of three simple strikes, we will double the drills tomorrow until your muscles learn obedience."

He stepped closer, standing near enough that his shadow completely engulfed the squire. He did not offer comfort. He did not ask what troubled the boy. 

"If they shake from some rot in your mind, master it," Kael continued, his gaze cold and unyielding. "A man who cannot command his own fingers to remain still has no hope of commanding a horse, a shield, or men-at-arms. The world does not care about your tempests, squire. It only demands that you stand."

He reached out, his heavy, leather-gloved hand coming down firmly on top of the squire's trembling knuckles. He did not squeeze to comfort; he squeezed to force the boy's grip to tighten and stabilize, physically imposing order on the shaking hands.

"The chapel bell is tolling. Whatever burden you carry, you lay it before the Creator at the altar, or you bury it in the dirt of this yard. You do not bring it to your duties."

He released the boy's hands and stepped back, his face a mask of gray stone.

"Sheathe the wood. Wash. I will not ask a third time."

**Squire** (turn 19):
*I flinch at his touch, then grip the sword tighter under his hand, trying to stop the tremor.* "Yes, Ser," I choke out, my throat tight. *I quickly sheathe the practice sword and hurry towards the well, trying to blink back the sudden sting in my eyes.*

**Ser Kael** (turn 20):
Ser Kael watched the boy's retreating back, his expression unchanged as the squire hurried toward the well. He had not missed the choked quality of the boy's voice, nor the sudden brightness in his eyes. Tears. 

To Kael, tears were worse than physical weakness. They were a waste of moisture, a useless surrender to self-pity that served only to blind a warrior when he most needed his sight. If the boy could not master his own humors, the first winter campaign would break him entirely. 

Turning back to the weapon rack, Kael systematically wiped down his own practice blade with a dry cloth, ensuring no moisture from the frost remained to rot the wood. He placed it precisely in its slot. He did the same for the squire's weapon, though he made a mental note to discipline the boy if he ever left his gear untended again. Today, the chapel bell took precedence.

He walked out of the training yard, his heavy boots striking the frozen earth in a slow, steady rhythm. 

Ten minutes later, Ser Kael stood just inside the arched stone entrance of the castle chapel. The air inside was thick with the scent of beeswax, drafty stone, and old incense. The local priest was already preparing the altar. Kael stood motionless near the heavy oak doors, his cloak draped perfectly, his hands folded over the pommel of his sword. 

He watched the entrance, waiting to see if his squire would arrive as ordered—clean, silent, and composed—or if he would prove himself unfit for the duty of the day.

**Squire** (turn 21):
*I burst through the chapel doors, slightly out of breath, my face still wet from the well. My clothes are straightened, and I try to look composed, but my eyes dart to Ser Kael, hoping I'm not late.* I bow my head, trying to be silent as I move to stand near him.

**Ser Kael** (turn 22):
Ser Kael did not turn his head as the squire entered, but his eyes tracked the boy’s hurried, breathless approach. The heavy oak doors clicked shut, the echo of the boy’s rushed footsteps dying out against the high stone vaulting of the chapel. 

Kael waited until the squire had taken his place beside him before he spoke. When he did, his voice was a low, dry whisper that barely carried over the soft hum of the priest’s pre-service preparations.

"You do not burst into the house of the Father as if you are chasing a stray hound," Kael said, his gaze fixed forward on the altar, refusing to look at the boy. "You enter with reverence. Your breathing is loud. Quiet it."

He noted the wetness on the squire's face. Whether it was the cold water of the well or the remnants of useless tears, Kael did not ask. It did not matter. The boy was here, and he was on time, even if only by the skin of his teeth. 

Kael stepped forward, his heavy boots making no sound on the stone floor—a silent, disciplined movement born of decades of practice. He crossed himself with a slow, deliberate motion, his gloved hand moving from forehead to chest, then shoulder to shoulder.

"You are within the mark of the bell. Barely," Kael murmured, his tone flat and empty of praise. "Kneel. We offer our prayers for the realm, our liege, and the strength to endure the winter. If you have personal griefs, leave them at the foot of the cross. Do not let them rot your focus."

With rigid, practiced grace, Ser Kael sank to one knee on the cold stone floor, his back perfectly straight, his hands folded over the pommel of his sword. He closed his eyes, his face settling into a mask of solemn devotion, completely ignoring the boy beside him as he began his silent prayers.

**Squire** (turn 23):
*I kneel quickly, trying to match his solemnity, but my knee cracks loudly on the cold stone.* My face flushes. *I try to slow my breathing, focusing on the priest's chanting, but my mind keeps drifting back to my father.*

**Kira** (turn 0):
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

**Captain** (turn 1):
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

**Kira** (turn 2):
"Shit," Kira muttered, but she was already moving. "You got it."

She shoved off from the boulder, breaking into a low, jagged sprint across the open shale. Her boots skidded on the loose scree, but she kept her center low, zigzagging hard between the sparse outcroppings beneath the eastern ridge to give the archers the widest possible target.

The thrum of bowstrings followed instantly. 

An arrow bit into the dirt an inch behind her heel. Another clattered violently off a slab of slate near her knee, throwing up a spray of stone chips. Kira didn't slow. She vaulted over a fallen trunk, landing in a slide that brought her behind a shallow rock shelf. 

"Come on, you bastards, earn your coin!" she barked toward the heights, just loud enough to draw their eyes. 

She peeked over the rim for a split second, twin daggers held ready in a reverse grip. Up on the east lip, three of the silhouettes had shifted their aim entirely toward her position, arrows knocked and tracking her sparse cover. 

"East side's looking at me, Cap!" she called out over the din, keeping her back pinned tight against the stone as two more shafts splintered against the rock above her head.

**Captain** (turn 3):
"Good. Keep them busy!" I yelled back, already halfway across the ravine. The sounds of battle were all around us now, a chaotic symphony of shouts, steel, and the thud of arrows. *I gripped my polearm tighter, scanning the western ridge for their archers.*

**Kira** (turn 4):
"Easy for you to say," Kira muttered through gritted teeth. 

The stone above her head cracked as another heavy broadhead sheared away a chunk of shale, showering her hair with dust. She didn't stay still. Staying still in a crossfire was just volunteering for a shallow grave. 

She timed the cadence of the bowstrings—two quick thrums, then a split-second lull as they reached into their quivers. 

*Now.*

Kira bolted from the shelf, staying low and cutting hard to the left across the loose gravel. She didn't run in a straight line, snapping her weight from side to side in erratic, jagged strides. 

*Thump. Skirr.* 

An arrow skipped off the scree right between her boots, kicking sharp gravel into her shins. Another tore through the loose edge of her leather mantle. 

"Fucking miserable shot!" she yelled up at the rim, flashing one dagger in a mocking salute before sliding on her knees behind a thick slab of granite nestled right up against the eastern wall's blind angle. 

Up close to the base, the ridge's overhang cut off their direct line of sight. The shafts stopped falling near her, replaced by frustrated shouts in a harsh dialect up above. 

Kira caught her breath, pressing her shoulder hard to the cold rock. She twirled the right dagger into a standard grip, eyes flicking upward to track the shifting shadows along the ridge. 

"They're leaning out to get an angle, Cap!" she hollered over the roar of the skirmish, her voice raw and carrying over the stone. "Two of 'em are moving south along the rim to flank my cover!"

**Captain** (turn 5):
An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

**Kira** (turn 6):
From her angle against the rock wall, Kira caught the glint of a broadhead pivoting away from her cover, locking straight onto the Captain out in the open scree. The archer was leaning hard over the eastern rim, fully drawing back the bowstring.

"Shit—Cap, high ridge!" she yelled.

There was no time to close the distance on foot. Kira broke from the safety of the overhang, stepped hard into the open, and whipped her right arm forward in a vicious, snapping arc. 

The dagger left her hand in a tight, whistling blur. 

Thirty feet up, the blade struck the archer's leather bracer with a dull, violent *clack*. The sheer kinetic force threw the man's lead arm wide, spoiling the release. The arrow snapped off erratically, skittering uselessly into the high ravine wall, while the archer stumbled back from the ledge with a sharp curse, clutching at his arm.

"Look at *me*, you bastard!" Kira snarled, already drawing a spare boot blade to replace the thrown steel. 

Her exposed move had cost her the element of surprise. Gravel rained down as the second archer on the southern rim whipped around, snapping an arrow onto the string and leveling it directly down at her chest. 

Kira dropped her weight instantly, bracing for the impact or the dive, her boots digging into the shale as she tracked the shooter's fingers on the release.

**Captain** (turn 7):
*I saw the dagger fly and heard Kira's shout.* The archer on the western ridge was still a threat, but I now had a moment. "Nice throw

**Kira** (turn 8):
The bowstring cracked. 

Kira didn't wait to see the flight path. She threw her entire weight into a hard sideways dive, tucking her shoulder as she hit the shale and letting the momentum carry her into a skidding roll. 

The heavy broadhead struck the stone where her torso had been a heartbeat prior, throwing up a shower of sparks and snapping the shaft in two. Sharp wooden splinters peppered the sleeve of her leather jack. 

"Don't thank me yet!" she yelled back over the chaos, rolling onto her boots and slamming her back hard against the base of the rock wall. 

Dust clogged her throat. She spat grit onto the stones, shifting the boot blade into a secure reverse grip alongside her remaining main dagger. 

Peering up past the lip of stone, Kira tracked the movement along the eastern rim. The archer she'd clipped with the thrown dagger was still hunched back, clutching his bleeding arm, while the other two scrambled along the rocky ledge to find a better vantage into the ravine floor.

"East ridge is losing their angle, Cap!" she called out, voice tight and rasping. "Two left up top on my side, repositioning! Western ridge is wide open for your push—move!"

**Captain** (turn 9):
I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

**Kira** (turn 10):
"Damn it," Kira hissed under her breath.

From her vantage across the ravine floor, the tactical picture turned sour in an instant. The vanguard had surged ahead along the lower gulley, leaving the Captain isolated against the western scree. Between them lay thirty yards of completely exposed, arrow-swept shale and a fresh tumble of loose rock—an impassable dead zone for a quick sprint.

Up above, the western ridge archers were clearly adjusting their sights toward the solitary figure below them.

"Cap! You're cut off from the vanguard!" she bellowed, her voice cutting sharp through the echoing clatter of the fight. "Western rim has the drop on your flank—two bowmen at your ten o'clock, high ledge!"

She couldn't cross the gorge without getting pinned in the open, but sitting idle wasn't an option. Kira shifted her weight, eyes rapidly mapping the jagged face of the eastern wall right beside her. Handholds were sparse—broken slate, jutting roots, and narrow seams in the rock—but if she could scramble up ten feet to a secondary ledge, she’d have a clean throwing angle across the gorge to harass the western archers.

"Hold that line!" she shouted across the expanse, slamming her daggers into her belt. 

She leaped, driving her boots into a narrow cleft in the stone, fingers digging deep into the cracked shale as she began clawing her way up the wall. Stones crumbled beneath her palms, but she hauled herself upward with gritty, frantic momentum, desperate to gain an angle before the western bowmen loosed.

**Captain** (turn 11):
*The western archers began to draw their bows, aiming at me.* "I see them, Kira! Just focus on your own flank!" I shouted, bracing myself for the incoming volley. *I had to find cover, fast.*

**Kira** (turn 12):
"Focus on my flank? Fine!" Kira spat, hauling her weight up over the lip of the stone ledge with a sharp grunt. 

Her elbows scraped raw against the slate, but she swung a boot up, finding purchase in a narrow groove and shoving herself flat against the shelf. The vantage gave her a sliver of cover from the west, but it put her dead underneath the remaining archers on the eastern rim.

Dirt and loose pebbles rained down onto her leather-clad shoulders—footsteps right above. 

"Fucking officers," she muttered under her breath, sliding both blades from her belt with a soft hiss of steel. 

She pressed her back hard into the vertical rock. Ten feet up from the ravine floor, the shelf was barely two feet wide, angling sharply toward a narrow fissure that cut into the eastern bluff. Up above, the silhouette of a bowman leaned out past the rim, peering straight down to track her climb, an arrow already nocked.

"Too slow, friend," Kira snarled.

Before the shooter could fully tilt the bow downward, she lunged upward from the ledge, driving the point of her right dagger violently into the man's overhanging boot. 

A choked howl echoed off the gorge walls as the archer jerked back, losing his balance and sending his arrow skipping wildly into the shale below. Kira ripped the blade free, resetting her footing instantly on the narrow ledge, her breathing hard and rhythmic through her teeth. 

"East side's down to one active bow on my head!" she shouted down into the ravine, keeping her blades up and her eyes locked on the rim above. "Still watching your back whether you like it or not, Cap!"

**Captain** (turn 13):
*I saw Kira's wild attack on the archer above her.* "Just stay alive, Kira!" I shouted back, already moving. *I spotted a small cluster of boulders ahead and sprinted for them, polearm ready.*

**Kira** (turn 14):
"Staying alive is in my damn contract!" Kira barked back, plastering herself against the stone wall as a heavy rock smashed into the ledge barely two feet from her boots, shattering into jagged shards.

Up above, the wounded archer had scrambled back, cursing in agony, but the last able-bodied eastern bowman was ditching his bow. Kira heard the scrape of steel clearing a scabbard directly overhead. 

They were done trading arrows on this side. They were coming to flush her out in close quarters.

"East rim's dropping the bows—they're drawing steel!" she shouted down over the rumble of the ravine. 

She didn't wait for them to find an angle down onto her narrow shelf. Sliding her daggers into a tight forward grip, Kira jammed her boots against the fissure's jagged lip and scrambled another four feet up the crevice, wedging her back against one wall and her knees against the other. It was tight, filthy, and entirely without cover, but it gave her leverage.

Across the ravine, the western ridge was still alive with movement, but Kira kept her eyes fixed upward on the rim above her head, waiting for the first silhouette to peer over the edge into her strike zone.

"You've got company coming on foot soon, Cap!" she called out, muscles coiled tight as gravel trickled down into her face. "Clear that western line before they regroup!"

**Captain** (turn 15):
"On it, Kira!" *I reached the boulders and immediately dropped to one knee, using them for cover.* I had to take out these western archers now.

**Kira** (turn 16):
A shadow fell across the crevice as the ambusher dropped down onto the ledge above Kira, a short sword already drawn and gleaming in the harsh daylight.

Kira didn't hesitate. The second his boots hit the stone, she uncoiled like a snapped spring. 

Pushing hard with her legs wedged against the fissure walls, she launched herself upward. The swordsman swung wide in the cramped space, the tip of his blade shearing uselessly into the shale wall with a harsh shower of sparks. Kira slid inside his reach, driving her left dagger up into the gap beneath his leather pauldron. 

The man grunted in shock, stumbling back against the cliff face. Kira slammed her full weight into his chest to pin him, twisting the blade and bringing her right dagger across in a brutal, tight slash. 

The swordsman collapsed with a wet heave, slumping against the narrow rock shelf. Kira yanked her blades free, her chest heaving as she wiped a streak of blood and stone dust from her eyes with the back of her sleeve. 

"One less on the east!" she called down, her voice rough and grating. 

She kicked the fallen weapon over the ledge, letting it clatter onto the ravine floor below. Leaning out just enough to scan the opposite side of the canyon, she tracked the western ridge. From her elevated perch, she could see the remaining bowmen up there leaning over their stone perches, frantically nocking arrows and trying to draw a bead around the boulder cluster.

"Cap!" Kira yelled across the gap, pressing herself against the blood-slicked stone to maintain her footing. "Two archers above you are leaning out to clear your boulder's blind spot! Hit 'em before they get the angle!"

**Captain** (turn 17):
"Got it!" *I said, already moving.* I burst from behind the boulders, polearm held high, and charged the nearest archer.

**Kira** (turn 18):
From her vantage up on the ledge, Kira tracked the explosive charge across the gorge. The western archers scrambled in a blind panic, their coordinated firing line collapsing the second the distance closed.

"Keep the pressure on 'em!" Kira yelled across the gorge, though her voice was half-lost to the roar of the melee.

She didn't linger to admire the push. Turning back to her own immediate problem, she hauled herself the final few feet up onto the flat lip of the eastern rim. Her knees took the brunt of the rough stone, but she was up in a crouch instantly, twin blades angled and ready.

The wounded archer she'd clipped earlier was on his knees twenty feet back, clutching his shattered forearm and frantically trying to scramble backward into the scrub brush. 

"Stay down or you lose the other one," Kira growled, stepping past him without breaking stride. 

She spotted her thrown dagger lodged in the dirt where the man had dropped his bow. She scooped it up in one fluid motion, wiping the gritty blade against her thigh before sliding the boot knife back into its sheath. 

A quick, sweeping scan of the eastern ridge showed the rest of the ambushers had broken ranks, scattering east into the rocky brush to escape the slaughter. The eastern high ground was clear.

Kira jogged to the rim, peering down into the ravine where the vanguard was mopping up the lower choke point, then swung her gaze across to the western slope.

"East ridge is broken, Cap!" she hollered down at the top of her lungs, daggers hanging loose at her sides as she caught her wind. "I've got the high ground secured! Vanguard is pushing through the gulley below!"

**Captain** (turn 19):
"Good work, Kira!" *I yelled back, my voice hoarse.* The western ridge archers were dealt with. *I looked down at the vanguard, then back at Kira.* "See if you can get eyes on the escape routes!"

**Kira** (turn 20):
